passage: Omkar, you look just like I did at ten. Let me tell you about the vase. My brother Ravi and I were wrestling when something crashed. Amma came running and shouted at me alone, because I was the elder boy. "It was Ravi's elbow!" I wanted to say, but my voice stuck in my throat. I stood there burning, and later I kicked Ravi's slippers under the bed. That night Amma sat beside me and asked, "What really happened?" She listened all the way through. I noticed that anyone who feels unheard just gets angrier, and at the wrong person. So when my grandchildren quarrel, I ask each child first. -- Hemant

qa.q: What were Hemant and Ravi doing when something crashed?
What did Hemant want to say when Amma shouted at him, and why could he not?
qa.a: He wanted to say it was Ravi's elbow, but his voice stuck in his throat because he was burning with the unfairness.

qa.q: What did Amma do later that made things better?
qa.a: She sat beside Hemant, asked what really happened and listened all the way through.

qa.q: What would change if Amma had asked both boys before scolding?
qa.a: Hemant would not have felt the burning unfairness or taken it out on Ravi's slippers, and both boys could have told their side.

grounding: An elder recalls being scolded unheard as a boy and how being asked later eased it.

passage:
"Payal, your Afreen Aunty knows how it feels to be blamed unfairly. When I was ten, my brother and I were fighting over a jar of pickle and it smashed on the floor.
My mother ran in, saw me standing there, and shouted at me. Only me. I tried to say my brother had pulled it too, but she said, 'Don't answer back!'
After that, I was so angry at my brother. We didn't speak for days.
Then Nani came to stay. She sat us both down and said, 'Now, each of you tell me what happened.' And we did. That was the first time I felt heard. After that, my brother and I stopped fighting so much."

qa.q: What broke when young Afreen and her brother fought?
How did young Afreen feel when her mother shouted only at her?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and unheard, which made her angry at her brother.

qa.q: Which turning point in the story helped the siblings?
qa.a: When Nani asked each child to explain what happened, so both felt heard and they fought less.

qa.q: How might young Afreen's brother have felt when only she was scolded?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved at first, but then guilty or distant, since they stopped speaking.

grounding: An aunt recalls her mother scolding her without hearing both sides, which made her angry at her brother, and how a grandmother asking each child helped.

passage:
The power was out and Mummy was rushing to light candles when she heard the crash. The new flower vase lay in pieces on the floor. Nitin was standing next to it. His younger brother Francis was on the sofa.
"Nitin! How many times have I told you to be careful?"
"But Mummy, Francis threw the ball!"
"Not now, Nitin! Clean it up."
Nitin's face burned. He glared at Francis.
Later, when the lights came back, Nitin said quietly, "Mummy, can I tell you what happened?"
She sighed and sat down. "Go on." She listened, then called Francis over. "Now you tell me."
Francis looked at the floor. "I threw the ball."

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when Mummy scolded only him?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and angry, glaring at Francis.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that helped?
qa.a: He waited until things were calmer and asked to explain, and Mummy then asked both boys.

qa.q: How might Francis feel when Mummy asks him to explain?
qa.a: Francis may feel guilty and nervous, looking at the floor as he admits the truth.

grounding: A mother scolds her older son without hearing both sides; he feels it is unfair, asks calmly to explain, and she asks each child.
